title: The pond, the road and a good-enough place
hookLine: the library gets loud, the coffee shop has a blender; Buddhaghosa on the pond, the fruit trees and the good-enough spot
carry: the buddha's fit place: not too far, loud or busy
tomorrow: a disc of clay. how could staring at it calm a mind?

lines: A BIRTHDAY PLAN, A BLENDER, A TV.
cards: The library is quiet until the table next to you starts planning a birthday. The coffee shop has great light and a blender. Home has the TV, and somebody asking where the scissors went.
Buddhaghosa has advice for anyone hunting for a place to sit, and it starts with yesterday's pond. A monastery near a pond, he says, is a poor choice, because people keep coming to draw water.
The same goes for fruit trees and flowering plants: they bring visitors. So does a road.

teach.b: His list of places to avoid reads like a list of interruptions. A big monastery, crowded with people. A new one, full of building work.
A crumbling one that always needs repairs.

teach.h: NOT TOO FAR, NOT TOO NEAR.
teach.b: One near a road, a city, a port or a border. A well-known one, where visitors keep arriving. Then he describes the good place, using the Buddha's own words from a sutta.
Not too far and not too near, with an easy path to it.

teach.h: QUIET AT NIGHT, PEOPLE TO ASK.
teach.b: Few people by day, little noise at night. Not much trouble from flies, mosquitoes, wind and sun. Basic needs easy to come by.
And people nearby who know the teaching, so you can ask them questions. Notice what he never asks for: perfect. Not too noisy, not too far, not too busy.
Not too is a forgiving phrase. Nobody here is required to find a mountain cave. So here's what the tradition hands you for this week.
Stop waiting for the ideal room and look for the good-enough one. A corner where nobody comes to draw water. A chair that faces a wall instead of the TV.
A suitable place, and then the same place again tomorrow.

how: Buddhist meditators may keep one regular spot for practice, at home or in a temple, and the Visuddhimagga advises choosing a monastery a little apart from busy roads and towns.

o: a perfectly silent room, far away from other people
a temple built to strict rules about its size and shape
a spot that's good enough: not too noisy, far or busy

games.q: the place and the problem — tap the pairs.

s: Buddhaghosa says a monastery near a pond is a poor place to practice
people keep coming to draw water, so there's no quiet.
by this teaching, the right place is a remote cave far from everyone
the sutta wants it not too far and not too near, with people nearby who know the teaching.
a well-known monastery is the best place to practice
fame brings visitors; Buddhaghosa lists it among the faults.

games.q: your friend says she can't start meditating until she's redone her whole bedroom into a calm space. what would Buddhaghosa say?
o: start in a good-enough corner now: not too noisy, not too busy.
she's right; the space has to be perfect before you begin.
the room never matters at all; only the mind matters.
games.why: Buddhaghosa takes the place seriously, so it isn't 'the room never matters'. but he asks for 'not too', not perfect.

practice: Sit where you might practice most days. Listen for the loudest sound there, then the quietest, and let both be.
Then make one small change to the spot, turn the chair, move a lamp, put the phone in a drawer, and sit the rest of the time in your slightly better place.

wordCard.voice: A suitable place: Buddhaghosa's good-enough spot for practice, not too far, not too noisy, not too busy.

orig.note: Pali: lodging, a dwelling place for practice; the sutta on the suitable place is named for it.

carryVoice: For the road: the Buddha's fit place, not too far, not too loud, not too busy, and good enough beats waiting for ideal. Five of forty, done.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IV.2–19 (the faults of an unsuitable monastery: largeness, newness, dilapidation, a road, a pond, leaves, flowers, fruit, fame, a city, timber, fields, incompatible people, a port, a border, and more; the suitable one)
Anguttara Nikaya 10.11, Senasana Sutta (the five factors of a suitable lodging)
